text: A plan you have never practised is a wish with bullet points.
note: Do one thing from your plan today — open the box, read the label, walk the route.

text: The cheapest water you will ever store is the water already in your pipes.
note: Fill the bathtub and every clean container the moment the power goes, not on day two.

text: Nobody panics about the thing they already know how to do.
note: Competence is the sedative. Practise the small tasks so the big day feels familiar.

text: Count how many steps from your door to the stairwell in the dark tonight.
note: Walk it once with a hand on the rail and note where the light switches are.

text: Store water where you will still be able to reach it when you are tired.
note: Pick a shelf at waist height in the hall, not the top of a closet.

text: Write down how much water your household actually drinks in a normal week.
note: Then buy one more than that and label every bottle with the date.

text: A pantry you cannot cook from is storage, not food.
note: Cook one full meal tonight using only what is in the cupboard and nothing else.

text: Buy the food you already eat, then eat it and buy it again.
note: Rotate one shelf this week so nothing in the cupboard outlives its date.

text: Know which room in your flat stays warmest before you need to know it.
note: Sit in each room for ten minutes tonight and notice the difference.

text: Blankets work better than bravado when the heating stops on a cold night.
note: Wash the spare blankets now so they are clean and dry when you want them.

text: A torch you cannot find in the dark is a torch you do not own.
note: Put one torch in the drawer you actually open when you walk in.

text: Charge the things you would miss first, not the things you use most.
note: Make a short list tonight of what needs charging and in what order.

text: Keep copies of your papers somewhere that is not your only flat.
note: Photograph your ID and lease today and send them to a relative you trust.

text: A document you cannot find is the same as a document you never had.
note: Spend ten minutes naming your scans properly so you can search them later.

text: A list of what your mother takes is worth more than a guess at a pharmacy.
note: Write the names and the prescriber's phone number on paper and keep it in your bag.

text: Keep the medication list where the ambulance crew would look, not in a drawer.
note: Tape a copy inside the front door cupboard and tell one neighbour it is there.

text: The neighbour who knows your name is worth more than a full cupboard.
note: Knock on one door this week and swap phone numbers with no other agenda.

text: Introduce yourself to the person across the hall before something goes wrong.
note: Ask whether they have a car, a landline, or someone who checks on them.

text: Practise the boring parts, because the exciting parts take care of themselves.
note: Time yourself finding the fuse box and turning off the water main.

text: A drill that takes an evening is cheaper than a week of learning in the dark.
note: Pick one Saturday and turn the power off for three hours on purpose.

text: Keep a small amount of cash at home in notes you can actually spend.
note: Break a note into smaller ones this week and put them somewhere dry.

text: Cards fail when the network fails, and the queue at the machine will be long.
note: Check what is in your wallet right now and whether any of it is paper.

text: You will make worse decisions tired, so protect the sleep you can get.
note: Keep earplugs and an eye mask in the bedside drawer where you can find them.

text: Sleep is not a luxury you can cut when the week gets strange.
note: Set a fixed bedtime tonight and keep it even if the evening is unsettled.

text: Children cope better with a plan they helped make than one handed to them.
note: Ask your child tonight what they would pack and write down their answer.

text: Give a child a job in a hard week and they stop being only frightened.
note: Let them own the torch, the list, or the door checking, and mean it.

text: Ask your father what he would do if the lift stopped working today.
note: Then ask who he would call, and make sure that number is written down.

text: An older parent on the fourth floor has a different plan from yours.
note: Walk their building this month and find the stairwell light and the exit.

text: Agree on one person outside the city who everyone will call.
note: Write that number on paper for every adult in the household this week.

text: Text messages queue and phone calls fail, so have more than one route.
note: Learn where the nearest working payphone or library phone is, just in case.

text: Learn where the water shut-off valve is before it is spraying the hall.
note: Find it tonight, turn it a quarter turn, and turn it back.

text: Know how to open your own front door when the lock will not turn.
note: Find the spare key you hid and either move it or tell one person.

text: A hand-crank radio is only useful if you know which station to find.
note: Tune it this week and write the frequency on a card beside it.

text: Fill the freezer with ice now and it will keep food cold later.
note: Freeze a few bottles of water tonight and leave space around them.

text: Cook once, portion twice, and the freezer becomes your second pantry.
note: Double tonight's dinner and label the extra portion with the date.

text: An apartment has less storage than a house, so choose what earns its space.
note: Empty one cupboard this weekend and put back only what you used.

text: The bag by the door should be small enough to carry down four flights.
note: Weigh it or walk it down the stairs and see how it feels.

text: Write the plan down because you will not remember it under pressure.
note: Put one page in the kitchen drawer and one in the hallway cupboard.

text: A list on your phone dies with the battery, so keep paper too.
note: Print the one page that matters most and fold it into your wallet.

text: Check your smoke alarm batteries on a date you will not forget.
note: Pick a birthday or a new year and test every alarm in the flat.

text: Learn to shut off the gas yourself, and know when to leave it alone.
note: Read the meter instructions once and take a photo of them.

text: A full fridge and an empty cupboard are two different kinds of hunger.
note: Check what in your kitchen needs power and what does not.

text: Buy the manual can opener, because the electric one only works sometimes.
note: Find it in the drawer and open one can with it tonight.

text: Keep a pair of shoes by the bed that you could walk a mile in.
note: Not slippers. Put real shoes there tonight before you sleep.

text: A phone with no charge is a paperweight with a screen and a battery.
note: Charge it before dinner, not before bed, and keep a cable by the door.

text: Keep a spare charger and a power bank where you sleep, not where you work.
note: Check the bank holds a charge and put it back where it belongs.

text: Write down the three things you would take, then check the list honestly.
note: If the list does not fit in one bag, cut it down tonight.

text: A neighbour with a spare key is a plan; a spare key under a mat is a hope.
note: Give the key to someone in the building and tell them when to use it.

text: Learn the sound your building makes when the power goes out.
note: Notice whether the hallway lights stay on and where the emergency lights are.

text: Keep a paper map of your own neighbourhood, because you know it less well than you think.
note: Mark the pharmacy, the school, the clinic and the nearest water tap.

text: Store water on the floor, not the top shelf, where a leak will not ruin everything.
note: Put the heavy bottles low and keep a towel and a small bucket beside them.

text: Ask yourself what you would do at nine in the evening with no lights and no lift.
note: Sit with that question for five minutes and write the first answer.

text: The best time to meet your neighbours is on a normal, unremarkable afternoon.
note: Say hello to two people in the hall this week and learn one name.

text: Keep the children's shoes and coats together so a cold exit is fast.
note: Move them to one hook by the door and put a torch beside them.

text: A written plan with names on it is a plan; the rest is a mood.
note: Write who does what on the back of the plan and sign it.

text: Check the expiry dates on the food you are keeping for an emergency.
note: Pull the oldest items to the front and cook one of them this week.

text: Give every adult in the flat the same information, not slightly different versions.
note: Read the plan aloud together and let each person correct you.

text: An emergency contact should be someone who answers on the first ring.
note: Call yours today and ask whether the number still works.

text: Know how long the water in your tank or boiler will last without power.
note: Fill the kettle and a jug tonight and see how far it actually goes.

text: A blanket, a torch and a radio will solve more nights than anything you can buy.
note: Put all three in one basket tonight so you stop hunting for them.

text: Ask the pharmacy how they would reach you if their systems went down.
note: Make sure they have a phone number that is not only your mobile.

text: Paper beats a dead battery, so write the numbers you would need down.
note: Copy the doctor, the pharmacy and one relative into the back of a notebook.

text: Practise carrying a full jug of water from the tap to the kitchen table.
note: You will spill less on a normal day than on a bad one.

text: Learn which of your neighbours has a car and which would need a lift.
note: Ask directly, once, and offer the same favour back without being asked.

text: A household that has talked about the hard week handles it better.
note: Have that conversation over dinner this week, before anything happens.

text: Keep the bin empty and the sink clear, because mess makes every problem worse.
note: Spend ten minutes tonight on the sink and the bin and nothing else.

text: Buy a second can opener and keep it in the drawer you would actually reach for.
note: Check the drawer now and buy the one thing that is missing.

text: A battery you bought three years ago is a decoration, not a supply.
note: Open the torch, look at the date on the batteries, and replace them.

text: Know where the nearest public tap or fountain is from your front door.
note: Walk it once this week and time yourself on the way back.

text: Write the plan for the person who is not you, because you may not be home.
note: Leave a copy where a babysitter or a relative would look first.

text: A child who knows the plan is calmer than a child who is being protected from it.
note: Explain the plan in plain words tonight and let them ask questions.

text: Keep one warm layer per person where you sleep, not in the hallway cupboard.
note: Put a jumper on every bed tonight and see whether anyone objects.

text: Keep a little cash where you can reach it without power or a network.
note: Count it tonight and replace anything you borrowed from it.

text: Check what your insurance covers before you need to make a claim.
note: Find the policy number today and put it with your other documents.

text: A phone tree with three names on it beats a group chat in a crisis.
note: Write the order down and tell each person who they call next.

text: Learn how to turn your phone into a hotspot before the wifi dies.
note: Try it once tonight and note how much battery it burns.

text: Keep a written list of what is in the freezer, because a cold box hides things.
note: Tape the list to the door and cross items off as you use them.

text: A quiet household is not a prepared one; check the things nobody has touched.
note: Open the cupboard nobody opens and see what is actually in it.

text: Take the stairs once this week so you know how many there are.
note: Count them, then decide whether you could do it carrying a bag.

text: Keep one folder for everyone's health paperwork and label it clearly.
note: Put the children's cards and the adults' cards in separate sleeves today.

text: Ring the bell of the person who lives alone and ask if they are alright.
note: Do it this week and leave your number on a slip of paper.

text: Preparedness is mostly knowing where things are and who to call.
note: Pick one thing you cannot find right now and give it a home.

text: A plan that depends on one person is a single point of failure.
note: Teach one other adult the water valve and the fuse box this month.

text: Write down what you would do first, second and third, then argue with it.
note: Read it back tonight and cut anything that needs two people.

text: The last thing you should be doing in the dark is looking for a torch.
note: Fix one torch to the inside of the hall cupboard tonight.

text: Learn the difference between a problem you can fix and one you should leave.
note: If you smell gas, leave, and call from outside rather than investigating.

text: Keep the hallway clear, because the exit is the part you cannot replace.
note: Move the buggy and the boxes tonight so the door opens fully.

text: A household budget that ignores the odd week is a budget for good weather.
note: Add one line tonight for the things you would buy in a bad week.

text: Teach the children how to call for help and what to say when they do.
note: Practise the address and the phone number out loud tonight, once.

text: The point of a plan is not to be ready for everything, only for the first hour.
note: Write what you would do in the first hour and keep it to one page.
